Particle Tracker in C++
Version 2.0.0

By Mohammad Yasir
IIT Delhi

PaTriC is an open-source, fully relativistic, multi-threaded charged particle tracker with support for arbitrary electric and magnetic fields. It utilizes the isolated particle model and thus, can simulate the motion of any number of charges in a given field configuration. All you need is a C++ compiler and PaTriC is yours to play with.

PaTriC is designed to be highly flexible and easy to use, allowing users to customize every aspect of the simulation and output. When you set up the simulation, you instruct PaTriC about the time-step, the integrator, the number of particles, the electromagnetic fields, and the data to output. PaTriC uses the specified integration algorithm to solve the equation of motion for the target particles using the Lorentz Force as the driving force. It then saves the variables you requested to simple, human-readable output files.

items.title: Features
items.text:
• Fully relativistic: The particle push algorithms available in PaTriC take the relativistic factor (gamma) into consideration while calculating the velocity updates. By default, the Boris push is used.
  • Multi-threading: By using OpenMP threads, PaTriC can track a large number of particles all at once, making it extremely suitable for nodes with large core counts.
  • Open-source: The entire codebase is available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 Licence.

items.title: Download
items.text: Download from GitHub

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
PaTriC ships with a few example scripts in the folder benchmarks that are used not only to benchmark but also to check for bugs and errors. Currently, the simplest cases have been provided as benchmarks, but more complex cases are in development.

This page will also be updated with performance metrics across multiple cores and nodes. Stay tuned!

items.title: Structure
items.text:
PaTriC uses C++ to setup your simulation. Example input.cpp and various benchmark files ship with the repository that you can copy and adjust for your use case.

When the program starts, it compiles the input file provided using the same compiler and compiler flags that were used to compile PaTriC itself. The input file must include the header patric.h that is installed with the program binary when you do make install.

The program then looks for a function called configureSimulation in the input file and calls it to set up the parameters of the simulation. This function takes various arguments, which are explained in the following sections. Overall, the function looks like so: 

void configureSimulation(Control*& ctrl, Particle*& prtcl, Fields*& fields, Output*& output) {
    // do stuff you need, define variables etc.
    ctrl   = new Control(timestep, simulationTime, particlePusher);
    prtcl  = new Particle(count, charge, mass, initialPositions, initialVelocities);
    fields = new Fields(electricFieldFunction, magneticFieldFunction);
    output = new Output(outputFileName, outputFilePath, outputFrequency, outputVariables);
}

items.title: Control
items.text:
The Control class contains information relevant to the setup of the simulation itself. This includes just three things:

  1. timestep: the time-step used by the integration algorithm.
  2. simulationTime: time till which the simulation will run for.
  3. particlePusher: the particle push algorithm to use. This must be either of Pusher::Boris [2], Pusher::Vay [3], or Pusher::HigueraCary [4]. A comparison of each of these algorithms is given in reference [1].

With the above variables, the control object is then initialized like so: 

ctrl = new Control(0.001, 1000, Pusher::Boris);

items.title: Particle
items.text:
This is a simple container for the target information. This includes:

  1. count: the number of particles to load and simulate.
  2. charge: the charge of the particle (in units of electron charge, see Units).
  3. mass: the mass of the particle (again in units of electron mass).
  4. initialPositions: the initial position of each of the particles.
  5. initialVelocities: the initial velocities of each of the particles.

items.title: Loading Initial Conditions
items.text:
The Particle() constructor expects std::vectors of Vector3D objects for the initialPositions and initialVelocities. For example, initialising a single particle at the origin with zero velocity looks like this: 

prtcl = new Particle(1, -1, 1, {Vector3D(0, 0, 0)}, {Vector3D(0, 0, 0)});

For a large number of particles, creating the vectors manually becomes cumbersome. The PaTriC header patric.h provides a few helpful functions to tackle this. They are outlined below:

items.title: getSameIC()
items.text:
Returns a vector containg the same values for all particles, which is to be provided as a Vector3D object. For example, to initialise 10 particles at the same position and velocity, you can do the following:

int particleCount = 10;
int particleCharge = -1.0;
int particleMass = 1.0;
prtcl = new Particle(particleCount, particleCharge, particleMass, 
        //x,y,z are the position coordinates.
        getSameIC(particleCount, Vector3D(x,y,z)),      
        // vx,vy,vz are the velocity components.
        getSameIC(particleCount, Vector3D(vx, vy, vz))  
    );

items.title: getRandomIC()
items.text:
Returns a vector of initial conditions, where each component has been randomly drawn from a uniform distribution between the provided limits.

prtcl = new Particle(particleCount, particleCharge, particleMass, 
        // Each particle gets a random position with components between the provided values.
        getRandomIC(particleCount, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax),             
        // For either of the directions, if upper and lower values are equal, the same value is assigned.
        getRandomIC(particleCount, vx_min, vx_max, vy_min, vy_max, vz_min, vz_max) 
    );

items.title: getRegularIC()
items.text:
Returns a vector where each component has been uniformly distributed between the provided limits. 

prtcl = new Particle(particleCount, particleCharge, particleMass, 
        getRegularIC(particleCount, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax),            
        getRegularIC(particleCount, vx_min, vx_max, vy_min, vy_max, vz_min, vz_max) 
    );  // Particles are spread evenly across the three-dimensional space.

items.title: getMaxwellianIC()
items.text:
It is also possible to get a vector of values that are spread with a given temperature. This depends on the particle mass and a Box-Muller transform is used to return thermally spread values centered on 0. 

std::vector<Vector3D> thermalSpread = getMaxwellianIC(particleCount, temperature, particleMass);

items.title: Fields
items.text:
The choice of the electric and magnetic fields is entirely arbitrary. They can be left blank to simulate the individual motion of each particle on its own. Once again, the following helpful functions from patric.h will be useful for this purpose. Each of these returns an std::function object that takes two arguments: the position at which to calculate the field, and the time at which to calculate it. The function returns the electric/magnetic field calculated at the provided location at the provided time. The object is initialized as: 

fields = new Fields(electricFieldFunction, magneticFieldFunction);

Info

For the ease of programming, this function is defined as a FieldGetter type in the header file. It is defined as typedef std::function<Vector3D(Vector3D, real)> FieldGetter;

Thus, each of the following inbuilt function returns an object of type FieldGetter.

items.title: Inbuilt Fields
items.text: The following helper functions may be used to setup the fields.

items.title: getConstantField()
items.text: Creates a function that returns the same, constant field everywhere at every time-step. Provide the value of this field into the argument as a Vector3D object.

items.title: getSineField()
items.text:
This functions takes the arguments \( (A, \omega, \phi, v, \hat{u})\) and returns a FieldGetter that calculates the field as:

\[ \vec{E} = A \sin (\omega \cdot v + \phi)\ \hat{u} \]

Here,

  • A: amplitude of field.
  • \(\omega\): angular frequency
  • v: the field is sinusoidal in this variable. Must be one of T, X, Y, or Z
  • \(\phi\): extra phase
  • \(\hat{u}\): unit vector along which, the field points.

items.title: getGaussianField()
items.text:
Takes the arguments \((A, \sigma, \mu, m, v, \hat{u})\) and returns a function that drives a gaussian/super-gaussian field using the formula:

\[ \vec{E} = A \exp (-(v-\mu)^m / 2\sigma^m)\ \hat{u} \]

Here, A, u, and v are same as before and

  • \(\mu\): the exponent for the gaussian
  • \(\sigma\): the standard deviation

items.title: Custom Fields
items.text:
If you want to define your own field, you can use the inbuilt FieldGetter type definition. It is created as follows: 

FieldGetter myCustomField = [](Vector3D position, real time) {
    // some work
    return Vector3D(x_component, y_component, z_component);
};

items.title: Output
items.text:
The output object contains information required to store the results of your simulation. Each particle gets its own file numbered from 0 through particleCount-1. Data is stored in tab-separated, human-readable .dat files. You can choose to provide a custom path for these files. The object is initialized as follows:

string outputFileName = "output";
string outputFilePath = "./data/";
unsigned int outputFrequency = 20;
vector<string> outputVariables = {POS_X, POS_Y, POS_Z, VEL_X, VEL_Y, VEL_Z};
output = new Output(outputFileName, outputFilePath, outputFrequency, outputVariables);

The first three arguments are self-explanatory. The program dumps the information requested via outputVariables vector (discussed below) at every outputFrequency-th iteration. To select which variables are dumped into the file, you can make use of pre-defined constants, which are listed below:

  • POS_X: particle's position - x component
  • POS_Y: particle's position - y component
  • POS_Z: particle's position - z component
  • VEL_X: particle's velocity - x component
  • VEL_Y: particle's velocity - y component
  • VEL_Z: particle's velocity - z component
  • GAMMA: particle's relativistic factor, calculated as \(\gamma = \sqrt{1 / (1 - (v/c)^2)}\)
  • E_FIELD_X: electric field experienced by the particle at that time-step - x component
  • E_FIELD_Y: electric field experienced by the particle at that time-step - y component
  • E_FIELD_Z: electric field experienced by the particle at that time-step - z component
  • B_FIELD_X: magnetic field experienced by the particle at that time-step - x component
  • B_FIELD_Y: magnetic field experienced by the particle at that time-step - y component
  • B_FIELD_Z: magnetic field experienced by the particle at that time-step - z component

items.title: Installation
items.text: The installation process has a few simple steps:

items.title: Get the prerequisites
items.text:
You will need:

  1. A C++ compiler that supports OpenMP. Most Linux systems ship with one by default, and you are free to choose whichever you find most suitable.
  2. An implementation of Make: The GNU Make that ships with most systems should suffice.

items.title: Get the code
items.text:
Clone the PaTriC repository into a folder of your choice:

git clone https://github.com/hafizmdyasir/PaTriC.git

items.title: Compile and install
items.text:
PaTriC's makefile expects the environment variables CXX and PREFIX to be defined and point to your C++ compiler binary and your preferred install location, respectively. The typical installation procedure looks like this:

cd patric
export CXX=g++
export PREFIX=/usr/local        # Requires sudo. Alternatively, install into $HOME/.local
make; make install

Info

By default, make will attempt to install into /usr/local and use g++ for compilation. You can override this by setting the environment variables CXX and PREFIX. Make sure to update the CXXFLAGS in the makefile accordingly.

items.title: Compilation Flags
items.text:
You can use the following parameters to control the compilation process:

  1. SI_UNITS: Do make SI_UNITS=true and PaTriC will use SI units for its calculations instead of normalized ones (see Units).
  2. HIGH_PRECISION/LOW_PRECISION: If either of these flags are set to true, then the calculation precision will be altered. HIGH_PRECISION corresponds to long double, while LOW_PRECISION corresponds to float. By default, double is used. Note that this behaviour is machine-dependent.
  3. DEBUG: For developers, this adds the flags -g -O0 to CXXFLAGS, allowing for easier debugging.

items.title: Run
items.text:
Open a terminal window and type patric. If everything has happened correctly, you should get the following output:

No configuration file specified. Program will exit.

In practice, you will need to provide the input script (see Input) as an argument to the program. You can also choose to run it with multiple threads or via mpirun (see Parallelization).

items.title: Multi - Threading
items.text:
The easiest way to parallelize your simulation is to use OpenMP threads. PaTriC uses OpenMP to parallelize the particle push algorithm, which is the most computationally expensive part of the simulation. This means that you can run your simulation on multiple threads and get a significant speedup.

This is achieved by setting the environment variable OMP_NUM_THREADS to the number of threads you want to use. For example, to run your simulation on 4 threads, you can do the following:

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=4
patric input.cpp

Doing so will divide the particles among the threads and each thread will push its own set of particles. This is a simple and effective way to parallelize your simulation, but it does have some limitations. For example, if you have a small number of particles, then the overhead of creating and managing threads may outweigh the benefits of parallelization.

Thread Count

Continuously increasing the number of threads will not necessarily yield maximum performance. The optimal number of threads depends on the number of particles as well as your CPU. You can use the command lscpu to see the number of cores available on your machine.

items.title: MPI Parallelization
items.text:
In Development

MPI parallelization is currently under development and will be available in a future release. This will allow you to run your simulation on multiple nodes and get even more speedup. Stay tuned!

The optimal MPI parallelization depends on the node/core configuration you are able to access. Typically, it is best to set the number of MPI processes to the number of sockets you have access to, and use the remaining cores for OpenMP threads. Do remember that these are suggestions and you can always experiment with different configurations to see what works best for your simulation.

2 Sockets, 16 Cores

If you have access to a node with 2 sockets and 16 cores, then you can run your simulation on 2 MPI processes and use 8 OpenMP threads per process. This should give you the best performance. 

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=8
mpirun -np 2 patric input.cpp

items.title: Basic Quantities
items.text:
The electron serves as our basis of normalization in PaTriC, where charge, mass, and velocity are normalized with respect to the electron charge, mass, and speed of light, respectively. This means that the charge of an electron is -1, its mass is 1, and the speed of light is also 1. A few derived quantities can then be defined:

  • Energy \(E_r = m_ec^2\)
  • Momentum \(p_r = m_ec\)
  • Temperature \(T_r = m_ec^2\)

items.title: Reference Quantities
items.text:
This alone is not sufficient for defining a complete system of units and for that purpose, one can select a reference frequency \(\omega_r\). Together with \(q\), \(m_e\), and \(c\), we can define a complete system of units. More often than not, it is convenient to select the reference frequency as the angular frequency of a known physical system.

For instance, if \(\omega_r\) is chosen as the angular frequency of electron in a uniform magnetic field of 1 Tesla, then the remaining quantities can be defined as follows:

Quantity Formula SI Units \(\omega_r\) (Angular Frequency) \(qB/m_e\) \(1.75 \times 10^{11}\) rad . s \(^{-1}\) \(T_r\) (Time) \(1 / \omega_r\) \(5.6875\) ps \(L_r\) (Length) \(c / \omega_r\) \(1.70625\) mm \(E_r\) (Electric Field) \(m_ec\omega_r/q\) \(3 \times 10^8\) V/m \(B_r\) (Magnetic Field) \(m_e \omega_r / q\) \(1\) Tesla

items.title: SI Units
items.text: You can also choose to use SI units in PaTriC. In this case, the compilation process changes slightly. Provide the parameter SI_UNITS=true to the makefile while doing make and it will take care of the rest.
